title: Fitbit daily resting heart rate by sex, 92,457 US adults, 2016-2018 (Quer et al. 2020, distribution digitised from Fig 2)

population.description: Fitbit users in the United States (all 50 states) who consistently wore a wrist heart-rate tracker. Starting from a convenience sample of 200,000 users, the authors kept 92,457 adults with a reported sex, age, and BMI who met the wear-time rules below. About 63% were women; average age was 45.8 years and average BMI 28.4 kg/m2 (as the paper reports them).
population.exclusions: Users who did not report sex, whose self-reported age was under 18 or over 100, or whose BMI (from self-reported height and weight) was outside 15 to 50 kg/m2; days with the device worn under 20 hours; users without at least 2 qualifying days per week for at least 35 weeks. No exclusion for medication or medical conditions is stated.

measurement.method: A single resting heart rate value per person per day, calculated by a proprietary Fitbit formula from interbeat intervals derived from the optical (PPG) sensor. The paper says this value is expected to represent the true resting heart rate that would be obtained supine immediately after waking, before getting out of bed, and that it was primarily calculated during periods of sleep.
measurement.device: Fitbit wrist-worn trackers: Charge HR versions 1 to 3 (65% of individuals), Blaze (21%), Alta HR (8%), Ionic (3%), Surge (2%), Versa (1%).
measurement.protocol: Continuous wear, with measurements obtained daily in normal living conditions. Only days with at least 20 hours of wear count. The mean in data.csv is the paper's mean RHR "for all individuals over all available monitored days" (median 320 days per person, maximum possible 730).

analysis: The paper's Fig 2 plots, for men and for women, the fraction of individuals at each whole beat per minute of their average daily resting heart rate, from 40 to 90. The height of each curve was measured at every whole value from 41 to 89.

The mean, SD, and percentiles here are computed from those measured fractions; none is printed in the paper. Each plotted value is treated as covering one beat per minute upward from that value, which is the reading under which the computed means match the dashed mean lines drawn in the figure.
Percentiles are interpolated linearly within each one-beat step. Values below 41 and above 89 are not shown in the figure; the measured fractions sum to 1.000 for each sex, so little lies outside.
n is the number of men (34,621) and women (57,836) stated in the figure caption.
use_for: The spread of wearable-reported resting heart rate by sex in a large group of adult Fitbit users: the only percentiles available for this kind of measurement in this entry.
Sizing a study of wearable-derived resting heart rate, with the caveat that this is a self-selected group of device owners.
do_not_use_for: A reference for a clinic pulse: the quantity, setting, and population all differ.
A distribution for the US general population: the cohort is unweighted device owners selected by wear-time rules.
Percentiles by age: the figure gives the two sexes only.
The distribution of a single day's value: each person contributes their average over many days, so this is the spread between people.
caveats: **Measured from a chart and then computed.** The percentiles are derived from curve heights read off the figure, not from the data. Treat them as good to about half a beat per minute.

**The half-beat alignment is inferred.** Whether a plotted value of 60 means 60.0 to 60.9 or 59.5 to 60.4 is not stated. The first reading is used because it reproduces the figure's own mean lines; the second would lower every value here by 0.5.
**Between-person spread of long-run averages.** A person's own day-to-day variation is not in these numbers.

**This is a wearable-derived daily value from a proprietary algorithm.** The paper states the formula is Fitbit's own and that the value is expected to represent a supine resting rate on waking; it is not a clinic measurement.

**Self-selected cohort.** The authors state the cohort "is not likely to be representative of the total socioeconomic and demographic diversity of the U.S." About 63% were women and the average age was 45.8; age was self-reported, BMI was calculated from self-reported height and weight, and sex was reported by the user.
**Strict wear-time rules.** People needed at least 2 days per week with 20 or more hours of wear for at least 35 weeks, which selects consistent users.

provenance.figure: Fig 2 (distribution of average daily resting heart rate for men and women)
provenance.method: Publisher's 2180 x 1512 pixel image; plot frame located in pixels (40 to 90 beats/min, 0 to 0.06 of individuals); each curve's vertical centre read at every whole beat per minute by colour
provenance.precision: about 0.5 beats/min for the percentiles and 0.1 beats/min for the means

verification: Four checks against numbers the paper states. (1) The measured fractions sum to 1.0000 for men and 0.9999 for women. (2) The computed means, 63.37 and 66.61, sit 0.06 and 0.08 below the dashed mean lines measured in the same figure (63.43 and 66.69). (3) The text says "95% of men had an RHR between 50 and 80 bpm, while the corresponding range for women was between 53 and 82 bpm"; the computed 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles are 49.8 and 79.6 for men and 53.0 and 81.9 for women. (4) Combining the sexes by the caption's counts gives a mean of 65.40 and SD of 7.62 against the text's "65.5 ± 7.7 bpm".
